title: East Asia: Song China and Its Neighbors
subject: AP World History

chunks.text: The Song Dynasty ruled China from 960 to 1279 CE. Historians divide it into the Northern Song (960–1127), with its capital at Kaifeng, and the Southern Song (1127–1279), with its capital at Hangzhou.

In 1127 the Jurchen people conquered northern China and founded the Jin Dynasty, forcing the Song court south. The smaller Southern Song that remained actually grew wealthier than before by emphasizing trade, agriculture, and manufacturing.

Around the year 1200, Song China was the richest, most populous, most technologically advanced, and most bureaucratically organized state in the world. Its southern capital, Hangzhou, held over a million people at a time when London had only about forty thousand.

Confucianism is a philosophy based on the teachings of Confucius (Kongzi), who lived around 500 BCE. It teaches that social order depends on people fulfilling their proper roles with virtue: rulers governing benevolently, subjects obeying, and children honoring their parents through filial piety.

Filial piety is the Confucian value of respect, obedience, and devotion that children owe their parents and ancestors. It served as a model for loyalty to rulers and order within the family and the state.

The Song civil service examination tested mastery of the Confucian classics and was used to select government officials. The Song greatly expanded the exam system to staff a professional bureaucracy of scholar-officials, also called the scholar-gentry.

The Song examination system created a partial meritocracy: in principle anyone could take the exams and rise through ability rather than noble birth, but years of study required tutors, books, and freedom from labor that only wealthier families could afford. It was more open than hereditary rule but not equal.

Neo-Confucianism was a revival of Confucian thought during the Song Dynasty that fused traditional Confucian ethics with metaphysical ideas borrowed from Buddhism and Daoism. It became the official state ideology and reinforced social hierarchy and filial piety.

Zhu Xi (1130–1200) was the leading thinker of Song Neo-Confucianism. His synthesis of Confucian ethics with Buddhist and Daoist metaphysics shaped the official ideology of China and later spread to Korea, Japan, and Vietnam.

Neo-Confucianism intensified the subordination of women, idealizing them as obedient wives and mothers. The elite practice of foot binding — tightly binding young girls' feet to keep them small as a painful mark of status — spread during the Song era and restricted women's mobility.

Champa rice was a fast-ripening, drought-resistant strain of rice introduced to China from the Champa kingdom in what is now Vietnam. Because it matured quickly, farmers could harvest two or three crops a year on the same land, driving a population boom.
Fueled largely by Champa rice, China's population roughly doubled during the Song era, climbing past 100 million — by far the largest population of any state in the world at the time.

The Song rebuilt and extended the Grand Canal, a vast inland waterway connecting the rice-rich south to the populous north of China. It allowed grain and goods to move cheaply across the empire and helped integrate a national market.

Song China was the first society to issue government-backed paper money at scale. Merchants also used letters of credit known as 'flying cash' to transfer value over long distances without hauling heavy copper coins, expanding commercialization.

Song ironworks, fired partly by coal, produced enormous quantities of iron and steel for weapons, tools, nails, and farm equipment. This output reached levels that Europe would not match for many centuries.

Song artisans produced fine porcelain and silk for export. Porcelain became so identified with the country that it is still called 'china' today, and these manufactured goods fueled trade across the Indian Ocean and Silk Roads.

Proto-industrialization refers to large-scale, market-oriented manufacturing that stops short of factories and steam power. Song China is described as proto-industrial because so much of its porcelain, silk, and iron was produced for sale rather than for the maker's own use.
China viewed itself as the Middle Kingdom, the center of the civilized world. This worldview shaped its diplomacy and its sense of cultural superiority over neighboring peoples.

The tributary system was an arrangement in which neighboring states sent gifts and acknowledged Chinese superiority in exchange for trade access and recognition. Foreign rulers gained access to China's wealth, while China gained prestige and a stable regional order.

Buddhism, which had entered China centuries earlier, remained influential during the Song, including Chan Buddhism (known as Zen in Japan). Buddhist metaphysical questions also influenced the development of Neo-Confucianism.

Korea, under the Goryeo dynasty, adopted Chinese models most fully, including Confucianism, a civil service examination, Chinese writing, and Buddhism. However, Korea's powerful hereditary aristocracy kept most high offices in noble families, so the exams never became a true ladder of social mobility.

Japan borrowed Chinese Buddhism, writing, and art during its earlier Heian period but rejected the centralized, exam-based bureaucracy. By the Song era Japan was developing feudalism, with real power held by the shogun, a military dictator, and a class of warrior-nobles called samurai.

Samurai were the warrior-nobles of feudal Japan, bound by a code of loyalty and honor later called bushido. Their dominance made Japanese society decentralized and militarized, almost the opposite of China's centralized civilian bureaucracy.

Vietnam, the kingdom of Dai Viet, adopted Confucian government, the civil service examination, and a tributary relationship with China, yet fiercely guarded its independence and repeatedly resisted Chinese political control. Vietnamese women retained more rights and social standing than Chinese Neo-Confucian ideals prescribed.

Although Chinese culture radiated across East Asia, Korea, Japan, and Vietnam each borrowed selectively and adapted Chinese models to local conditions. China set the cultural menu, but each neighbor adopted different elements in different ways, making this a key example of cultural diffusion and comparison.

The Song idea that government posts should be earned by examination rather than inherited by nobility influenced the wider world. European observers later studied the Chinese exam system, and modern civil-service examinations trace part of their lineage to Song China.
